t: Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain
w: Short essays on what a brain is actually for. Her answer: mostly running the body's energy budget, by predicting what is coming rather than reacting to it. It changes how a bad day reads. A heavy mood is often the body's budget running low (sleep, food, people, movement), not a verdict on your life.
h: Barrett's view that emotions are built by the brain rather than triggered as fixed programmes is one side of a live scientific debate, and she says so.
r: One lesson per sitting. Each is about twenty minutes.

w: A funny, careful book about why people are bad at predicting what will make them happy: we imagine the future with the details missing, and we underrate how quickly we adapt. Useful when a decision or a fear about the future feels bigger than it will turn out to be.
h: Some studies it leans on are single experiments from the 1990s and early 2000s. The central finding, that we overestimate how long feelings will last, has held up well.

t: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat
w: A neurologist's stories about patients whose brains work differently after illness or injury. Each one shows how much of an ordinary self rests on machinery we never notice until it changes. Humane, curious, and easy to read one story at a time.
h: These are clinical stories, not studies. Some readers and disability writers have criticised how Sacks portrayed his patients.
r: Read any single story. They stand alone.

w: Why looking inward gives such unreliable answers about why we feel and act as we do, and what works better: watching what you actually do, keeping a record, and listening to people who see you. It is the readable version of the research on the self shelf.
h: Written by one of the researchers whose work it reports, so it is a strong case for one view. The core findings on the limits of introspection are among the best replicated in psychology.

t: Being You: A New Science of Consciousness
w: A neuroscientist's account of the self as the brain's best guess: about the world, about the body from the inside, and about who you are. It makes feelings like dread or flatness easier to see as perceptions, which can be questioned, rather than facts.
h: Seth argues for one framework (perception as prediction). It is influential, not settled, and other researchers disagree.

w: A Nobel laureate's tour of the shortcuts the mind takes: fast intuitive judgement and slow deliberate thought, and where each goes wrong. Good for noticing when a confident inner voice is guessing.
h: Long. The chapter on priming relies on studies that later failed to replicate, and Kahneman publicly acknowledged this in 2017. Read it selectively and skip that chapter.

w: Argues that there are no hidden depths behind our thoughts: the mind improvises, moment by moment, and the inner story is made up as it goes. Unsettling at first, then oddly freeing: if your past moods do not define a fixed inner nature, you are less stuck than you feel.
h: Deliberately provocative. Many psychologists think it overstates a real finding.

t: Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy
w: Cognitive therapy explained for the reader, with exercises for catching the thoughts that drag a mood down (all-or-nothing thinking, mind reading, labelling yourself) and answering them. Practical rather than reflective.
h: One of the few self-help books tested in controlled trials: reading it helped people with mild to moderate depression (Scogin and colleagues, 1989, and later studies). It is dated in places and long; use the exercises, skim the rest. It is not a replacement for a doctor when things are bad.
r: Start with the chapter on the ten thinking errors and try one exercise, not the whole book.

w: An introduction to acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT): making room for difficult thoughts and feelings instead of fighting them, and doing what matters to you anyway. Plain, kind, and short on jargon.
h: ACT as a therapy has a good record in trials for low mood and anxiety. The book itself has been tested less than the therapy.

w: On treating yourself the way you would treat a friend having a hard time, and why that is different from self-esteem or letting yourself off the hook. Includes short practices.
h: The questionnaire behind much of this research is debated (see the entry on the practice shelf). The idea is simple and the book repeats itself in places.

w: A short memoir of depression and anxiety in his twenties and how he came through, written in very short chapters. Many readers say it was the first thing that made them feel understood.
h: One person's experience, not a guide or a treatment. It describes suicidal thoughts directly near the start, so choose a steady day for it.

w: A novelist's account of a severe depression that hit him at sixty: how it arrived, how it felt from inside, and how he recovered. Under a hundred pages and precise about something that is hard to put into words.
h: Frank about severe depression and suicidal thinking. Read it on a steady day, not a heavy one.

w: A psychologist who studies mood disorders writes about living with her own bipolar illness. She sees it from both sides, as the scientist and as the patient, which makes it unusually clear about moods, medication and identity.
h: About bipolar disorder specifically. Still useful if that is not yours, for how she separates herself from her moods.

t: The Noonday Demon: An Atlas of Depression
w: Part memoir, part reporting: depression across history, cultures and treatments, alongside his own episodes. The most complete single book on the subject for a general reader.
h: Long, and the treatment chapters date from 2001. Chapters stand on their own; read the one that fits the question you have.

w: The private notebook of a Roman emperor, reminding himself how to live: what is in his control, how to deal with difficult people, how small any one day is. Written for nobody, which is why it still reads as honest.
h: Stoicism is a philosophy, not a therapy. The founders of cognitive therapy named it as a forerunner, which is a historical link, not evidence.
r: A page a day. The Gregory Hays translation (2002) is the most readable modern English.

w: A short letter arguing that life is long enough if you do not give it away to busyness and other people's demands. Takes under an hour.
h: Written by a very rich man whose own life did not always match his advice; read it as advice, not as a model.

t: Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals
w: An average life is about four thousand weeks. Burkeman argues that accepting you cannot do everything is a relief rather than a defeat, and that the aim is to choose what to neglect. Warm and funny.
h: A book of argument and personal experience, not research.

w: A philosopher's plain, witty look at the everyday causes of unhappiness (boredom, envy, a sense of sin, fear of other people's opinion) and what tends to help (interest in things outside yourself, affection, work). He writes from his own unhappy youth.
h: Nearly a century old and of its time in places. The core advice, turn attention outward, matches later research on rumination.

t: How to Live: A Life of Montaigne in One Question and Twenty Attempts at an Answer
w: A life of Montaigne, who invented the essay by writing about himself honestly, organised as twenty answers to the question of how to live. A friendly way into someone who spent his life trying to understand his own mind without a system.
h: A biography with a point of view. Bakewell is clear about which answers are Montaigne's and which are hers.

t: Life Is Hard: How Philosophy Can Help Us Find Our Way
w: A philosopher who lives with chronic pain writes about illness, loneliness, failure, grief and the feeling that life does not add up, and what careful thinking can and cannot do about them. Honest about the limits of consolation.
h: Philosophy, not psychology: it offers arguments, not measured effects.

w: A psychiatrist's account of surviving the Nazi camps, and his argument that people can bear almost anything if it has a meaning for them.
h: Some historians have questioned details of his account. The therapy he founded (logotherapy) has little trial evidence. The memoir part is the reason to read it.

w: The original attempt to understand yourself by writing honestly about your own habits, moods, body and doubts, without a system. Wandering, frank and often funny.
h: Long and old. Do not read it in order.
r: Start with the last essay, Of Experience.

w: Three short essays by a novelist and philosopher arguing that how we attend to other people and to the world, patiently and without the ego in the way, is most of what a good life is.
h: Dense; each essay rewards a second read.

w: Camus asks what to do when life does not seem to have a meaning given from outside, and answers: live anyway, fully and in revolt. The famous last line imagines Sisyphus happy.
h: It opens by calling suicide the one truly serious philosophical problem. On a heavy day, choose something else.
